section: Why Not Just Use PubMed Alerts?
text:
Why Not Just Use PubMed Alerts?
PubMed alerts are a reasonable starting point, but they have a key limitation: they give you a flat, unsorted list. If you set up an alert for “inflammatory bowel disease,” every matching paper arrives in the same inbox pile - therapeutics next to epidemiology next to basic science - and you still have to read through everything to find what’s relevant to your work.
IBD LitMonitor takes a different approach. Instead of delivering a raw feed, it organizes papers into sub-fields so you can go straight to the topic area you care about and skip the rest. Each category is collapsible, so browsing the day’s literature takes minutes rather than a lengthy inbox triage.

Keeps public history focused on published artifacts.

NoteHow to Read This Report



Coverage: PubMed queries across a broad set of IBD topic groups, deduplicated - each paper appears exactly once in the most specific matching category.
Categorisation: Automatic and imperfect - a paper found by multiple queries is assigned to the most specific one (e.g. a vedolizumab trial in children goes to Pediatric IBD). For keyword search across all categories or papers from the past 30 days, use the Interactive Dashboard.
Study design badges RCT Meta-analysis Review are shown only when PubMed has explicitly assigned a publication type. Papers published within the last 1-2 weeks often don’t have a badge yet.
★ Flagship journals: Papers from Gut, Gastroenterology, Lancet, NEJM, JCC, and other leading GI journals are marked ★.

Sabachvili M, Abbott S, Thomson C, Davoli Ferreira M, Ohland C, Fritscher J, Gekeler C, Tricomi M, Müller P, Drikic M


DOI: 10.1136/gutjnl-2026-339262  |  View on PubMed →





Effects of Two Lactobacillus Strains on Aloe Vera-Induced Melanosis Coli in Guinea Pigs and Their Potential Mechanisms.  Probiotics and antimicrobial proteins  |  2026-11-12



This study primarily elucidated the efficacy of Lactobacillus plantarum P-8 (P8) and Lactobacillus acidophilus 85 (LA85) against melanosis coli (MC), a non-inflammatory bowel disease characterized by colonic mucosal lipofuscin deposition, currently lacking specific therapeutic interventions. The MC guinea pig model was established via 8-week intragastric administration of Aloe Vera (AV). Colonic tissues were harvested after 4 weeks of daily oral Lactobacillus gavage. Gross observation, H&E staining, and Fontana-Masson staining were employed to assess therapeutic efficacy. Western blotting and TUNEL staining were utilized to evaluate apoptosis of intestinal epithelial cells. Gut microbiota was analyzed by 16​S rRNA sequencing, and GC-MS was used to quantify short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) levels. P8 and LA85 significantly alleviated MC in guinea pigs, with effective reduction in melanosis area, restoration of colonic tight junction protein expression, and inhibition of intestinal epithelial cell apoptosis. Additionally, P8 and LA85 supplementation ameliorated gut microbiota composition, exhibiting increased abundance of Parabacteroides and Rikenellaceae_RC9_gut_group with reduction in norank_f__Eubacteriaceae. Furthermore, P8 supplementation was associated with significant reductions in the fecal levels of acetic acid, propionic acid, butanoic acid, valeric acid, and isohexanoic acid, whereas LA85 did not significantly alter the measured SCFA levels. P8 and LA85 significantly alleviated MC with inhibition of intestinal epithelial cell apoptosis and modulation of gut microbiota composition. These findings provide a scientific basis for utilizing P8 and LA85 as potential nutritional supplements in MC treatment.


Li D, Zhou L, Wu Q, Fang Y, Wang T, Kang L, Li Y, Yin Z, Zhang J


DOI: 10.1007/s12602-026-11287-1  |  View on PubMed →





Cadmium sulfide nanoparticles exacerbate colitis via Faecalibaculum rodentium-mediated modulation of the indole-3-lactic acid-Th17 axis.  Chemico-biological interactions  |  2026-11-11



With the increasing application of cadmium sulfide nanoparticles (CdS-NPs), their potential adverse effects on intestinal health have attracted growing attention. However, the impact of CdS-NPs exposure on inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we demonstrate that daily oral gavage exposure to 1 mg/kg CdS-NPs for 4 weeks or 11 weeks alone did not induce apparent colonic inflammation in healthy mice but exacerbated both acute and chronic DSS-induced colitis, as evidenced by severe weight loss, increased disease activity, colon shortening, tissue damage, and immune infiltration. Integrated gut microbiota profiling and metabolomic analysis revealed that CdS-NPs markedly reduced the abundance and tryptophan-metabolizing capacity of Faecalibaculum rodentium (F. rodentium), leading to impaired indole-3-lactic acid (ILA) production. F. rodentium administration significantly alleviated CdS-NPs-aggravated DSS-induced colitis and restored serum ILA levels, accompanied by suppression of Th17 responses. Consistently, exogenous ILA treatment attenuated intestinal inflammation and suppressed Th17/IL-17 responses in vivo and inhibited Th17 differentiation in CD4+ T cells in vitro. Collectively, our findings identify microbial tryptophan metabolism and IL-17 signaling as critical mediators of intestinal inflammatory sensitization associated with CdS-NPs exposure and highlight the F. rodentium-ILA axis as a potential intervention target for CdS-NPs-induced intestinal inflammation.


Ni S, Xu S, Zhang Z, Pei W, Yuan W, Kadier D, Peng K, Liu X, Zhang Z, Li L


DOI: 10.1016/j.cbi.2026.112432  |  View on PubMed →





Hyaluronic acid-grafted pH-responsive microcarriers for CD44-targeted co-delivery of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG and its extrusion-derived bacterial membrane vesicles to rebalance intestinal homeostasis.  International journal of pharmaceutics  |  2026-11-11



Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) stems from gut dysbiosis, impaired intestinal epithelial barriers and persistent mucosal immune dysfunction. Free oral probiotics or probiotic-derived extracellular vesicles yield poor therapeutic effects against IBD, as they degrade rapidly in the gastrointestinal tract and lack specific tropism for inflamed colon lesions. To overcome these delivery limitations, we fabricated pH-responsive hyaluronic acid (HA)-decorated alginate microcapsules (ALHA@LGG&EBMVs) to co-deliver viable Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) and extrusion-derived bacterial membrane vesicles (EBMVs). The electrosprayed Ca2+-crosslinked alginate skeleton confers robust gastric-acid protection, and surface-immobilized HA enables specific binding to CD44 overexpressed on inflamed colon epithelium. In vitro simulated gastric fluid assays revealed that the ALHA shell afforded superior protection to encapsulated LGG and EBMVs. In vivo fluorescence tracing on dextran sulfate sodium-induced colitic mice showed ALHA@LGG&EBMVs achieved 2.7-fold higher cargo accumulation at inflammatory colon sites with 24 h prolonged lesion retention relative to untargeted cargo-loaded alginate microcapsules (AL@LGG&EBMVs). In vivo therapeutic assays verified that the dual-cargo microcapsules mitigated colitis symptoms, restored epithelial tight junctions and reduced excessive intestinal epithelial permeability. Mechanistic studies revealed concurrent improvements across three key pathological dimensions: balancing the abnormal Th17/Treg ratio, promoting anti-inflammatory M2 macrophage polarization, and remodeling dysbiotic gut microbiota to expand beneficial commensals and reduce the abundance of pro-inflammatory pathobionts, which collectively facilitate the restoration of intestinal homeostasis. This polysaccharide delivery system integrates gastric-acid shielding and active inflammatory-lesion targeting to achieve multi-dimensional restoration of intestinal homeostasis. This proof-of-concept study offers a biocompatible microecological nanomedicine prototype for IBD intervention and establishes a blueprint for the development of oral gut-targeted biomaterials.


Ji Q, Chen H, Sun X


DOI: 10.1016/j.ijpharm.2026.127656  |  View on PubMed →





Dsg2 truncation causes a severe intestinal epithelial barrier breakdown and alters microbiome and immune response.  JCI insight  |  2026-11-10



Inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) including Crohn’s disease (CD) are characterized by impaired intestinal epithelial barrier (IEB) function. Alterations in the desmosomal cadherin desmoglein 2 (Dsg2) have been linked to loss of IEB and intestinal inflammation in IBD. We investigated the pathogenic impact of a cytoplasmatic-truncating mutation in the desmosomal cadherin desmoglein 2 gene (DSG2) in an IBD patient. Genetic analysis of a CD patient revealed a likely pathogenic DSG2 mutation leading to a truncated protein lacking part of the intracellular domain. Generation of an enterocyte-specific mouse model to recapitulate the human mutation resulted in a lethal intestinal barrier defect which was evident in homozygous but not in heterozygous mice. In vitro, barrier defects correlated with changes in Dsg2 mobility and upregulation of pore-forming tight junction protein claudin-2. Organoids derived from heterozygous Dsg2 truncated mice exhibited increased epithelial susceptibility to proinflammatory cytokines. Bulk RNAseq followed by gene ontology analysis in homozygous mice revealed a skewed IL17/IL23 response overlapping with transcriptional changes in patients with CD. Furthermore, 16S rRNA sequencing revealed alterations in microbiome composition in animals that carried the Dsg2 truncation. In summary, a patient-derived mutation in the DSG2 gene causing cytoplasmic truncation in homozygous state induced a lethal intestinal barrier breakdown in mice paralleled by altered gut microbiota and intestinal immune response.


Kugelmann D, García-Ponce A, Thielemann N, Radeva MY, Anders M, Kang DE, Siadjeu C, Burkard N, Horn AK, Neubauer J


DOI: 10.1172/jci.insight.183554  |  View on PubMed →





Microbiome changes following immigration: Rethinking “Westernization” as an explanatory concept.Review★  Gut microbes  |  2026-11-10



An emerging focus in microbiome science is on changes to people’s microbiomes following immigration, particularly to so-called Western countries, such as the USA, Canada, and Australia. Moving to these regions has been linked to microbiome changes that may increase immigrants’ susceptibility to health problems, including obesity and Inflammatory Bowel Disease. The term “Westernization” (and adjacent terminology) is frequently used to describe changes in diet, lifestyle, and built environment - and the consequent microbiome shifts - associated with immigration. However, what Westernization means in this context, and whether it is an appropriate descriptor, is often unclear. The purpose of this article is to provide a review of the diverse meanings associated with the terms “West”, “Western”, “Westernization” (and similar) across microbiome-related research and broader uses. We argue that these terms can obscure the specific structural, environmental, and cultural factors shaping microbiome changes. We discuss the consequences of this imprecision and provide recommendations for future research. Avoiding oversimplified conclusions about what impacts immigrants’ microbiome and health can contribute to more accurate targets for public health interventions for these groups in the long term.


Sharma R, Holcomb LE, Ishaq SL, O’Doherty KC


DOI: 10.1080/19490976.2026.2756705  |  View on PubMed →





The Microbiota-Metabolism Axis: Mechanistic Insights and Translational Targets Across Diabetes and Gastrointestinal Disorders.Review  International journal of endocrinology  |  2026-11-09



The gut microbiota (GM) modulates host energy balance, glucose-lipid metabolism, and enteroendocrine signaling through metabolite-receptor axes that include short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) acting on FFAR2/FFAR3 (GPR43/GPR41), microbially transformed bile acids signaling via FXR/TGR5, and amino-acid/choline-derived compounds such as imidazole propionate (ImP) and trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO). These pathways regulate incretin biology (GLP-1/PYY), insulin sensitivity, hepatic glucose output, adipose lipolysis, and appetite, thereby shaping risk and progression of Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), obesity, inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), and related conditions. Here, we synthesize mechanistic and translational evidence, highlight bidirectional drug-microbiome interactions (GLP-1 receptor agonists), and review interventions spanning diet, pre/probiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), and pharmacologic targeting of bile-acid and SCFA pathways. Together, these findings support precision strategies that profile GM-metabolite signatures (e.g., SCFAs, secondary bile acids, and ImP TMAO) to guide prevention and therapy in metabolic and gastrointestinal disease.


Akif A, Sultana N, Mikrani I


DOI: 10.1155/ije/7761643  |  View on PubMed →





A homogeneous acidic polysaccharide from Guangxi-cultivated Alpiniae Oxyphyllae fructus attenuates DSS-induced ulcerative colitis by remodeling the amino acid metabolism-microbiota-barrier axis.★  International journal of biological macromolecules  |  2026-11-06



Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic intestinal inflammatory condition with limited management options, driving interest in food-derived bioactive polysaccharides as potential dietary interventions. Alpiniae Oxyphyllae Fructus (AOF), an edible and medicinal plant traditionally used for gastrointestinal health, is widely cultivated in Guangxi, China; however, polysaccharides from Guangxi-grown AOF have not been systematically characterized, and their structure-activity relationships in UC remain undefined. In this study, a homogeneous acidic polysaccharide (AOFP-3) was isolated from Guangxi-cultivated AOF and structurally characterized. Its anti-UC activity was evaluated in a dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced mouse model by integrating untargeted metabolomics, targeted amino acid profiling, 16S rRNA sequencing, and immunohistochemistry. AOFP-3 was identified as a highly branched acidic heteropolysaccharide (Mw 19.728 kDa) rich in galacturonic acid (53.38%), with a putative backbone of alternating →4)-α-D-GalpA-(1 → and →4)-α-D-GalpA-6-OMe-(1 → residues. In DSS-induced UC mice, AOFP-3 dose-dependently alleviated weight loss, colon shortening, histopathological damage, and inflammation. Mechanistically, AOFP-3 treatment was associated with restoration of amino acid homeostasis, particularly involving branched-chain amino acids and the alanine/glycine-serine-threonine metabolic axis, with remodeling of the gut microbiota (enrichment of Akkermansia and Lactobacillus and suppression of Staphylococcus and Enterococcus) and repair of both physical (Occludin, Claudin-1, ZO-1) and chemical (MUC-2, goblet cells) barriers. These findings establish a structural and mechanistic basis for the bioactivity of Guangxi-grown AOF polysaccharides and support their further investigation as functional food ingredients for gut health promotion.


Xiang Y, He C, Yuan H, Wang E, Yan Z, Li Z, Liu C, Zhang Y, He J


DOI: 10.1016/j.ijbiomac.2026.155156  |  View on PubMed →





Fecal neuraminidase correlates with inflammatory signatures and microbiome shifts in preclinical Crohn’s disease.★  Gut microbes  |  2026-11-05



The mucus layer, rich in mucin glycoproteins, serves as a critical barrier to microbial invasion. Neuraminidases cleave terminal sialic acids from mucin glycans, a process that may influence mucus integrity, epithelial exposure to microbial antigens, and mucosal immune responses, making fecal neuraminidase activity a biologically relevant functional readout of host-microbe interactions in the context of Crohn’s disease (CD) pathogenesis. We evaluated whether fecal neuraminidase activity is associated with future CD risk and examine its relationships with inflammatory and microbial signatures relevant to early disease development. Within the prospective GEM cohort, 69 individuals who later developed CD were matched to 69 healthy first-degree relative controls. Fecal neuraminidase activity was measured using a fluorometric assay. Conditional logistic regression assessed its association with future CD risk. Partial Spearman correlations evaluated relationships with 446 serum proteins (OLINK), followed by pathway enrichment analysis, and with fecal calprotectin (FCP) and gut microbial composition (16S rRNA sequencing). Fecal neuraminidase activity was positively associated with future CD (OR = 1.541; 95% CI: 1.05-2.25; p = 0.026). Proteins correlated with neuraminidase activity were enriched in immune and inflammatory pathways. Neuraminidase activity was positively correlated positively with FCP (p ≤ 0.05), and its association with future CD was attenuated after adjustment for FCP. Fourteen microbial taxa were significantly correlated with neuraminidase activity (q ≤ 0.05). Fecal neuraminidase activity’s relationships with inflammatory markers and microbial taxa support its potential relevance as a functional marker of host-microbe alterations during preclinical CD.


Mu K, Dang CP, Xue M, Li Q, Huynh HQ, Griffiths AM, Turner D, Moayyedi P, Steinhart AH, Dieleman LA


DOI: 10.1080/19490976.2026.2755166  |  View on PubMed →





Bile acid dysmetabolism and microbial dysbiosis coincide with Clostridioides difficile infection in pediatric inflammatory bowel disease.Review  Npj gut and liver  |  2026-11-05



Pediatric inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients are at increased risk for Clostridioides difficile infection. This review highlights bile acid dysmetabolism, driven by gut microbiota dysbiosis and reduced microbial production of secondary bile acids, as a key factor linking pediatric IBD to increased CDI susceptibility. We examine interactions among IBD, dysbiosis, bile acid metabolism, and C. difficile, and discuss emerging microbiome-based interventions aimed at restoring bile acid homeostasis.


Rowe JC, Winston JA


DOI: 10.1038/s44355-026-00084-w  |  View on PubMed →





Caffeic acid regulates the gut microbiota-tryptophan metabolic axis to improve intestinal barrier function and relieve ulcerative colitis.★  Phytomedicine : international journal of phytotherapy and phytopharmacology  |  2026-11-01



Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease for which current therapies remain inadequate. Caffeic acid (CA), a natural hydroxycinnamic acid polyphenol, possesses anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties. However, whether CA engages the gut microbiota-tryptophan-aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AHR)-Nrf2 axis in UC has not been established. To evaluate the anti-UC activity of CA in vivo and in vitro and to elucidate its underlying mechanisms through a multi-platform integrative strategy. A dextran sulfate sodium (DSS)-induced murine colitis model and lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-stimulated mouse colonic epithelial cells (MCECs) were used in parallel. Mechanism was addressed by combining microbiota, metabolomic, transcriptomic and proteomic profiling with faecal microbiota transplantation, computational and biophysical target validation, and siRNA-mediated AHR knockdown. CA was administered at 10 and 20 mg/kg/day, with 5-aminosalicylic acid as positive control. Complementary platforms included 16S rRNA gut microbiota sequencing, untargeted serum metabolomics, colonic transcriptomic profiling, data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry proteomics, human UC single-cell RNA sequencing (GEO: GSE214695), faecal microbiota transplantation into antibiotic-pretreated recipients, molecular docking, 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation, cellular thermal shift assay, dual-luciferase reporter assay, and co-immunoprecipitation. CA dose-dependently alleviated dextran sulfate sodium-induced colitis, suppressed NF-κB activation, and reduced interleukin-6, interleukin-1β, and tumour necrosis factor alpha. Gut microbiota profiling revealed enrichment of Bifidobacterium and Dubosiella with depletion of Escherichia-Shigella. Transplantation of the CA-remodelled microbiota into antibiotic-pretreated recipients reproduced the protective phenotype and restored colonic AHR and cytochrome P450 1A1 expression, demonstrating that the remodelled community is sufficient to confer protection. Metabolomics showed enrichment of serotonin-branch tryptophan metabolites, with 5-hydroxytryptamine among the most significantly enriched differential metabolites. Molecular docking and 100 ns molecular dynamics simulation indicated stable binding of CA within the AHR ligand-binding domain, cellular thermal shift assay confirmed intracellular target engagement, and a dual-luciferase reporter assay demonstrated concentration-dependent activation of dioxin response element-driven transcription, establishing CA as an AHR agonist. CA increased Nrf2, NQO1 and HO-1 and restored Claudin-1, Occludin and zonula occludens-1; AHR knockdown reduced these effects and the suppression of NF-κB, indicating that both actions depend on AHR. CA ameliorates UC through convergent AHR activation, arising from both microbiota-mediated tryptophan reprogramming and direct receptor binding, with AHR-dependent Nrf2/NQO1/HO-1 induction and NF-κB suppression to restore intestinal barrier integrity. These findings support CA as a multi-target phytochemical candidate for UC treatment.


Lin X, Alioui Y, Wang W, Wu L, Ao J, Yan C, Liao J, Wang Z, Wu Y, Feng Y


DOI: 10.1016/j.phymed.2026.158905  |  View on PubMed →





Synbiotic of 2’-FL and B. longum subsp. infantis BXY2 Alleviates Colitis in Toddler Microbiota-Associated Mice: Potential Involvement of Gut Microbial Arachidonic Acid Metabolism.  Journal of agricultural and food chemistry  |  2026-11



Increasing inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) incidence in toddlers requires safe interventions. We developed a synbiotic combining 2’-fucosyllactose (2’-FL) with Bifidobacterium strain and evaluated its protective efficacy against DSS-induced colitis in toddler microbiota-associated (TMA) mice. Among 30 Bifidobacterium strains, Bifidobacterium longum subsp. infantis BXY2 and Bifidobacterium. breve BG4 utilized 2’-FL in vitro. However, only the 2’-FL and BXY2 synbiotic significantly alleviated colitis. The 400 mg/kg 2’-FL and BXY2 synbiotic showed the greatest protective effect, restoring body weight and colon length, reducing disease activity and histological scores, improving barrier function, attenuating inflammation. Compared with 2’-FL or BXY2 alone, the synbiotic enhanced goblet cells and barrier proteins. Metagenomics revealed enrichment of B. longum subsp. infantis and Phascolarctobacterium faecium. Metabolomics showed reduced fecal arachidonic acid (AA). These results indicated that gut microbial AA metabolism might be involved in alleviating colitis in TMA mice. Thus, this synbiotic is a promising preventive strategy for toddler IBD.


Jing Y, Bai X, Li J, Feng X, Gu Y, Ji Y, Zhai Z, Hao Y


DOI: 10.1021/acs.jafc.6c11011  |  View on PubMed →

Flares occurred after embryo transfer during established pregnancy (gestational week ≥8), with no flares occurring during or immediately following oocyte retrieval. Secondary endpoints showed low rates of new corticosteroid use (2.7%), IBD-related hospitalizations (0.7%), and medication dose escalation (0.7%). Among the 63 embryo transfers, biochemical pregnancy occurred in 63.5% (n = 40 of 63) and live births in 42.9% (n = 27 of 63). Across all 149 ART encounters, patients with IBD demonstrated low flare risk and live birth rates comparable to the general population. Under multidisciplinary guidance, ART is a safe and viable option in IBD.
